title: Five months of worsening breathlessness in a 72-year-old smoker with COPD
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 72-year-old man with COPD and a 50 pack-year smoking history, brought to the ED with 5 months of worsening breathlessness, weight loss, haemoptysis and a hoarse voice. The candidate then interprets his observations, ECG, bloods and chest X-ray, which shows a large right pleural effusion. They give a justified differential diagnosis, outline the pleural investigations and management, and safety-net.
focus: Subacute breathlessness: eliciting the red flags for lung cancer, examining for and interpreting a large pleural effusion, and planning pleural fluid analysis and work-up
stem: You are the intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Sam Herman, a 72-year-old man, has come in by ambulance with shortness of breath. He is sitting up on a trolley in an acute bay, on a monitor, with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken his observations, recorded an ECG, sent bloods and requested a chest X-ray.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sam and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, ECG, blood results and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sam Herman, a 72-year-old retired mechanic. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are thin, sitting bolt upright and breathless. Speak in short sentences and pause to catch your breath. Your voice is hoarse. You are very anxious. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Sam came in by ambulance about 20 minutes ago. At triage his resp rate was 27, sats 92% on room air, heart rate 104 and regular, BP 148/86, temp 37.6. The repeat just now was resp rate 29, sats still 92% on room air, heart rate 110, BP 144/84. The paramedics didn't give him oxygen. The ECG is done, bloods have gone and the chest X-ray is on its way."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they sit you right up or lean you forward on a table, you feel a little easier.
  • If they ask the nurse for oxygen, the nurse asks: "He has COPD. What saturation target would you like?" If they say 88 to 92% and ask for oxygen only if he drops below that, the nurse agrees and his sats stay at 92%. If they ask for high-flow oxygen through a mask without a target, the nurse repeats the question.
  • If they explain calmly what they are doing, you settle a little. If they use jargon, ask what it means.
  • If they ask for the X-ray, bloods or a scan now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I've been feeling very short of breath, doc. I can't breathe properly."

History (give only when asked):

The breathlessness

  • It has come on gradually over 5 months and keeps getting worse.
  • It is worse when you move about. Resting helps only a little. Your COPD puffer does not help at all.
  • Now you are breathless even sitting still and walking around the house. Before this you could climb a flight of stairs without stopping.
  • You are not sure what caused it. "I just thought it was my lungs getting worse."

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Weight: you have lost about 20 kg over the same 5 months without trying (from about 82 kg to 62 kg). Your clothes are hanging off you.
  • Appetite: poor. You are not hungry.
  • Sputum: you have always had a smoker's cough in the morning with a little white phlegm. For the last few weeks there have been streaks of blood in it.
  • Voice: it has gone hoarse over the last couple of months.
  • Sweats and fevers: you wake drenched in sweat at night, and you have had chills and some fevers.
  • General: you feel run down and tired all the time.
  • No chest pain, including no pain when you breathe in. No sick contacts.
  • No new wheeze. No change in the amount or colour of the phlegm apart from the blood. No drowsiness or confusion.
  • You sleep on two pillows, as you always have. You do not wake up gasping at night. No ankle swelling.
  • No calf pain or swelling. No palpitations, no fainting.

Past medical history

  • COPD.
  • Type 2 diabetes.
  • High blood pressure.
  • No cancers and no operations.
  • Immunisations up to date (flu, pneumonia and COVID vaccines).

Medications

  • Trelegy Ellipta (fluticasone furoate, umeclidinium and vilanterol), one inhalation daily.
  • Salbutamol (Ventolin) puffer when needed; you have been using it more but it does not help.
  • Metformin.
  • Irbesartan.
  • No blood thinners, no aspirin, no over-the-counter medicines.

Allergies: none.

Family history

  • Mother, 92, has dementia and diabetes.
  • Father died at 75 of a heart attack.
  • Brother, 67, has had a heart attack and a stroke.
  • No lung cancer in the family that you know of.

Social history

  • Smoking: 20 cigarettes a day for 50 years. You still smoke.
  • Alcohol: 3 beers a day. No recreational drugs.
  • Work: retired mechanic. Only if asked about work exposures: you spent decades working on brake pads and clutches and never wore a mask. You do not know if there was asbestos in them. No known exposure to radon, and nobody else smokes at home.
  • TB exposure: only if asked: born in Australia, never lived or travelled in a country with a lot of TB, no known contact with TB, never had TB or a positive TB test.
  • Home: you live alone. Your children live nearby and you see them regularly. You are reasonably well connected.
  • Low activity. A poor diet with a lot of takeaway.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you do not know what is causing this. You are very anxious, and your main concern is that you cannot breathe. You want something done so you can breathe easier.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "I just can't get my breath, doc. It's frightening."

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: thin and cachectic with temporal wasting (62 kg). Sitting upright, using his neck muscles to breathe, speaking in short sentences. Hoarse voice. Not cyanosed. Not drowsy.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: finger clubbing. Heavy nicotine staining. No asterixis. Warm, capillary refill 2 seconds.
  • Neck: a hard, non-tender 1.5 cm lymph node in the right supraclavicular fossa. No other nodes. JVP not raised.
  • Trachea: deviated to the left.
  • Respiratory: expansion reduced on the right. Stony dull percussion on the right from about the 2nd intercostal space anteriorly (mid-scapula posteriorly) down to the base. Breath sounds absent and vocal resonance reduced over the dull area, with bronchial breathing just above it. Left side resonant with vesicular breath sounds and a prolonged expiratory phase, no wheeze or crackles.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no added sounds.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. No hepatomegaly, no ascites.
  • Legs: no oedema, calves soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Sam's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
Recognises that he is breathless and very anxious: sits him upright, keeps questions short and focused, acknowledges his fear and explains what is happening in plain words.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual over 5 months and steadily worsening
Exercise tolerance: now breathless at rest and walking around the house; previously climbed a flight of stairs without stopping
Modifiers: worse on exertion, rest helps only slightly, his COPD inhaler does not help

check.x: Elicits the red flags for lung cancer:
check.d: Credit when the weight loss and the blood-stained sputum are found, plus at least one other kid.

kids.x: Unintentional weight loss of 20 kg over 5 months, with loss of appetite
Night sweats, chills and fevers, malaise and fatigue

check.x: Screens for differentials in at least three systems: heart failure (orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling), COPD exacerbation (change in cough, sputum or wheeze, drowsiness or confusion) and pneumonia (pleuritic pain, sick contacts). All are absent apart from the blood in the sputum and the fevers.
Quantifies smoking: 20 a day for 50 years (50 pack-years), still smoking.

Asks about other lung cancer and pleural disease risk factors: occupational exposure (decades on brake pads and clutches as a mechanic, a possible asbestos exposure), passive smoke, radon, and a family history of lung cancer.
check.d: Credit when the occupational or asbestos exposure is elicited, plus at least one other risk factor.

check.x: Takes the past medical history: COPD, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, no previous cancer or surgery, immunisations up to date.
Takes the medication history (Trelegy Ellipta, salbutamol reliever, metformin, irbesartan) and confirms he takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet, which matters before a pleural procedure.
Asks about allergies: none.
Takes a family history: mother 92 with dementia and diabetes, father died at 75 of a heart attack, brother 67 with a past heart attack and stroke.
Takes a social history: 3 beers a day, retired mechanic, lives alone with children nearby, low activity, poor diet with regular takeaway.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause, very anxious, main concern is the difficulty breathing, wants to breathe easier.
Examination

General inspection and vital signs: cachexia, sitting upright, accessory muscle use, speech in short sentences, hoarse voice, cyanosis, and the nurse's observations (RR 29, SpO2 92% on room air, HR 110).
Examines the hands and finds finger clubbing and nicotine staining; notes that COPD alone does not cause clubbing.
Palpates the cervical and supraclavicular nodes and finds a hard right supraclavicular node.
Examines the chest and identifies a large right pleural effusion:

kids.x: Stony dull percussion on the right from about the 2nd intercostal space down
Absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance over the dull area; left side resonant with vesicular breath sounds

check.x: Looks for heart failure and fluid overload as a cause of an effusion: JVP, heart sounds, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly and ascites (all normal).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone with a worsening RR and a rising heart rate (white zone), needing clinical review. Notes that SpO2 92% on room air is within his COPD target of 88 to 92%.
Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia at about 106/min with no ischaemic changes and no arrhythmia.

Interprets the bloods. Normal hs-troponin and NT-proBNP argue against ACS and heart failure. Mild normocytic anaemia, thrombocytosis, a raised CRP and low albumin fit chronic illness, malignancy or poor nutrition. Normal INR and APTT, an adequate platelet count and normal renal function make pleural aspiration and contrast CT safe. The venous gas shows no hypercapnia.
check.d: Credit when normal cardiac markers, the anaemia, thrombocytosis, CRP or low albumin, and safety for the procedure are mentioned.

check.x: Interprets the chest X-ray as a large right pleural effusion (meniscus to the 2nd anterior rib) with mediastinal shift to the left and a clear left lung, and states that a CT is needed to see the underlying lung.
check.d: Credit when the large right effusion and the shift to the left are stated.

check.x: Gives the leading diagnosis as a malignant right pleural effusion, most likely from primary lung cancer. Justifies it with the gradual breathlessness, 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, hoarse voice, clubbing, supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years.

Names the differentials with a feature for or against each: mesothelioma (possible asbestos exposure), parapneumonic effusion or empyema (fevers, but no pleuritic pain and a normal WCC), tuberculosis (night sweats and weight loss), and heart failure (no orthopnoea or oedema, normal NT-proBNP).
check.d: Credit when at least three differentials are named, each with a feature from this patient.

check.x: States that the fluid must be sampled to classify it as an exudate or a transudate, using Light's criteria with paired serum protein and LDH.
Management

Escalates to the senior ED doctor or medical registrar. Sits him upright with continuous monitoring. Gives oxygen only to keep SpO2 at 88 to 92% because he has COPD, and avoids high-concentration oxygen.

Arranges an ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration by an experienced clinician, after consent and confirming normal clotting and no anticoagulant. It is both diagnostic and therapeutic, removing no more than 1.5 L at one time.
Sends the pleural fluid for:
check.d: Credit when protein, LDH and cytology are included plus at least one other kid.

kids.x: Appearance, protein and LDH (with serum levels for Light's criteria)
Gram stain and culture, with acid-fast bacilli microscopy and culture

check.x: Requests a contrast CT of the chest (and upper abdomen), ideally before the effusion is fully drained, to look for a primary tumour, nodes, pleural thickening and metastases.
Admits under the respiratory or general medical team and refers to the lung cancer MDT for a tissue diagnosis.
Offers supportive care: nicotine replacement in hospital and Quitline, dietitian review for the weight loss, and social work or OT review because he lives alone.
Safety netting

Answers "Is it cancer?" honestly and kindly: cancer is a real possibility but is not confirmed until the fluid and scan results are back. Explains the next steps in plain words, checks understanding and offers to involve his children.

Tells Sam in plain words to tell the nurse at once if he has worse breathlessness, chest pain, more than streaks of blood in his sputum, or feels faint. After the fluid is drained, he should report chest tightness, a cough that won't settle or new breathlessness.
Arranges follow-up: fluid and CT results reviewed by the inpatient team with a lung cancer MDT plan; explains the fluid can come back and to return to ED (or call 000) if the breathlessness returns.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, the ECG the nurse recorded, his blood results and the chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask this only after the examiner reads question 4:

  • "Is it cancer, doc?"

You are frightened. If the candidate is honest and kind, you accept the plan, and if they offer to call your children, you agree. If they use jargon, ask what it means. If they say flatly that it is definitely cancer, or that it is definitely nothing, look worried and ask: "How can you know that already?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets taken on room air before any treatment; the 10:55 set was taken just before you arrived.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage RR 27 and SpO2 92% on room air are in the yellow zone. HR 104, BP 148/86 and temperature 37.6 °C are white. At 10:55 RR is 29 (yellow, rising), SpO2 is still 92% (yellow) and HR has risen to 110 (white).
  • Meaning: he is tachypnoeic and mildly hypoxic with a worsening trend, which fits a large effusion compressing the right lung. SpO2 92% is within his COPD target of 88 to 92% (TSANZ), so he does not need oxygen yet. A white-zone heart rate does not mean he is well.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, here a senior review now, with repeat observations. Draining the fluid is what will relieve his breathing. Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 88%. A move into the red zone (RR 30 or more, or SpO2 below his target) calls for a rapid response; ask the senior to document altered calling criteria for SpO2 consistent with the 88 to 92% COPD target.

rows.note: Triage after ambulance arrival: to acute bay, sitting upright, ECG requested
Repeat set at bedside before medical review

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Mr Sam Herman, age 72, recorded at 10:45 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 106/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia. Regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +70°.
  • PR interval: 160 ms.
  • QRS duration: 90 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 440 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression. T waves upright apart from aVR.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves. No P pulmonale. No low voltage. Normal R wave progression.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 106/min with a normal axis and normal intervals. No ST or T wave changes, no Q waves, no arrhythmia and no low voltage.
  • Meaning: the tachycardia fits his breathlessness and hypoxia. There is no evidence of ischaemia or of atrial fibrillation as a cause of his breathlessness, and nothing to suggest a large pericardial effusion.
  • Changes: no cardiac cause is found to treat. The work-up focuses on the chest.

handover.label: Bloods and venous gas
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 118 g/L with a normal MCV is a mild normocytic anaemia. Platelets 468 are raised. WCC and neutrophils are normal and CRP is 38. Sodium 134 is mildly low. Albumin 29 is low. Serum protein and LDH are recorded for comparison with the pleural fluid. Creatinine and eGFR are normal. hs-troponin and NT-proBNP are normal. INR and APTT are normal. The venous gas is normal, with a pCO2 of 42 and no acidosis.
  • Meaning: anaemia, thrombocytosis and a raised CRP with low albumin fit a chronic illness such as malignancy, along with poor nutrition. A normal WCC argues against empyema, but does not exclude it. The normal troponin and NT-proBNP argue against ACS and heart failure. The albumin is not low enough to explain a large effusion. There is no hypercapnia.
  • Changes: normal INR and APTT, an adequate platelet count and normal renal function make pleural aspiration and contrast CT safe. Keep the serum protein and LDH for Light's criteria.

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, erect PA view. Mr Sam Herman, 72, taken today at 11:05.

Clinical details: 72-year-old man, current smoker (50 pack-years) with COPD. 5 months of worsening breathlessness, weight loss and blood-tinged sputum. SpO2 92% on room air.

Findings:

  • Technical: adequate inspiration on the left, not rotated, adequate penetration.
  • Pleura: large right pleural effusion with a meniscus extending to the level of the right 2nd anterior rib. The right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are obscured. No pneumothorax.
  • Lungs: the left lung is clear, with a sharp left costophrenic angle. The aerated right upper zone is clear. The underlying right lung cannot be assessed.
  • Heart and mediastinum: the trachea and mediastinum are shifted to the left. The right heart border and right hilum are obscured by fluid, so heart size cannot be fully assessed. The left hilum is normal.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no destructive rib lesion seen. Reduced soft tissue bulk.

Conclusion: large right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift to the left. Left lung clear. Recommend pleural fluid sampling and CT chest with contrast to assess the underlying lung, pleura and mediastinum.
handover.model:
• Read: confirms the patient, date and an erect PA film. There is a large right pleural effusion with a meniscus up to the 2nd anterior rib, obscuring the right hemidiaphragm, right heart border and right hilum. The trachea and mediastinum are shifted to the left. The left lung is clear with no blunting of the left costophrenic angle, and there is no pneumothorax.
  • Meaning: a large unilateral effusion explains the right-sided signs, his hypoxia and his breathlessness. A unilateral effusion with weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness, clubbing, a supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years makes a malignant pleural effusion from lung cancer the top differential. Heart failure usually causes bilateral effusions with a large heart and upper lobe diversion.
  • Changes: he needs ultrasound-guided aspiration for diagnosis and symptom relief, and a contrast CT of the chest to look for the primary tumour.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sam Herman, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sam now, here in the emergency department, including the investigations you would arrange.
Sam asks you, "Is it cancer, doc?" Please answer him, then tell me what warning signs you would teach him and what follow-up you would arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Sam Herman, 72.
  • Situation: large right pleural effusion; RR 29 and SpO2 92% on room air (yellow zone, worsening), HR 110.
  • Background: 5 months of progressive breathlessness, now at rest; 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, hoarse voice; 50 pack-year current smoker, retired mechanic; COPD, diabetes, hypertension; no anticoagulants; lives alone.
  • Assessment: clubbing, hard right supraclavicular node, signs of a right effusion; ECG sinus tachycardia only; troponin and NT-proBNP normal; mild anaemia, thrombocytosis, CRP 38, albumin 29; clotting and renal function normal; no hypercapnia; CXR shows a large right effusion to the 2nd anterior rib with mediastinal shift to the left; left lung clear; underlying lung not seen. Likely malignant effusion.
  • Recommendation: please review; ultrasound-guided aspiration, contrast CT chest, admission.

Malignant pleural effusion from primary lung cancer: gradual breathlessness, 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, hoarse voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve; inhaled corticosteroid dysphonia is a benign alternative, but new hoarseness persisting beyond 3 weeks in a smoker is a red flag), clubbing, supraclavicular node, 50 pack-years, unilateral effusion.

  • Mesothelioma: for: possible asbestos from brake pads; needs CT and pleural biopsy.
  • Parapneumonic effusion or empyema: for: fevers, chills, CRP 38; against: 5-month course, no pleuritic pain, normal WCC.
  • Tuberculous effusion: for: night sweats, weight loss; against: Australian-born, no TB travel, contacts or past TB; needs AFB testing.
  • Heart failure (transudate): against: no orthopnoea, PND or oedema, JVP normal, NT-proBNP normal, unilateral effusion.
  • COPD exacerbation: against: no sputum change or wheeze; does not explain the effusion.

1. Senior review; sit upright; continuous monitoring; oxygen only to keep SpO2 88 to 92% (COPD).
  2. Ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration by an experienced clinician, with consent. Clotting is normal and he takes no anticoagulant. It is diagnostic and therapeutic, removing no more than 1.5 L at a time.
  3. Fluid: appearance; protein and LDH with serum levels (Light's criteria); pH and glucose; cell count and differential; cytology; Gram stain and culture; AFB.
  4. Contrast CT chest (and upper abdomen), ideally before full drainage.
  5. A chest drain and antibiotics if the fluid is pus or the pH is below 7.2 with suspected infection.
  6. Admit under respiratory or general medicine; refer to the lung cancer MDT for a tissue diagnosis.
  7. NRT, dietitian, social work.
  8. Optional extra: if malignant and recurrent, an indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis.

• Honest and kind: fluid around the right lung is pressing on it. Cancer is a real possibility given the weight loss and blood, but it is not confirmed until the fluid and scan results are back. Explains in plain words, pauses, checks understanding, offers to call his children.
  • Tell the nurse at once: worse breathlessness, chest pain, more blood in the sputum, feeling faint; after the drain, chest tightness, a cough that won't settle or new breathlessness.
  • Follow-up: fluid and CT results reviewed by the inpatient team with a lung cancer MDT plan. The fluid can come back: after discharge, return to ED or call 000 if the breathlessness returns.
  • Optional extras: GP letter; Quitline.

ddx.dx: Malignant right pleural effusion from primary lung cancer
ddx.for: Five months of progressive breathlessness with 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, a hoarse voice, clubbing, a hard right supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years, with a large unilateral right effusion on X-ray.
ddx.against: No tissue diagnosis yet; the fluid cytology and CT are still needed.

ddx.for: Decades of work on brake pads and clutches as a mechanic, with possible asbestos exposure, and a large unilateral effusion with weight loss.
ddx.against: Haemoptysis, a hoarse voice and a supraclavicular node point more to a primary lung cancer.

ddx.for: Fevers, chills, night sweats and a CRP of 38 in a man with COPD.
ddx.against: The 5-month gradual course, no pleuritic pain or sick contacts, and a normal white cell count.

ddx.for: Night sweats, fevers, weight loss and blood-tinged sputum with a unilateral effusion.
ddx.against: Born in Australia with no TB travel, contacts or past TB, and the smoking history and node make cancer more likely.

ddx.dx: Pleural effusion from congestive heart failure
ddx.for: Age, hypertension, diabetes and a strong family history of coronary disease.
ddx.against: No orthopnoea, PND or ankle swelling, JVP not raised, normal NT-proBNP, and the effusion is large and on one side only.

ddx.for: Known COPD with worsening breathlessness and a current smoking history.
ddx.against: No change in his cough, sputum or wheeze apart from the blood, his inhalers do not help, and it does not explain the right-sided dullness.

guide:
In Part 1, Sam answers the history and the nurse gives the opening observations. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Give the supraclavicular node only if the candidate palpates the neck or the nodes, and the clubbing only if they examine the hands. If the candidate asks for the X-ray, bloods, CT or a pleural tap in Part 1, say these will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Sam asks his one question ("Is it cancer, doc?") after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate settles a frightened, breathless man and keeps questions short. They characterise 5 months of progressive breathlessness and elicit the red flags: weight loss, blood-tinged sputum, hoarseness and night sweats. They screen heart failure, COPD exacerbation and pneumonia, quantify 50 pack-years and ask about asbestos at work. On examination they find clubbing, the supraclavicular node and a large right effusion. In Part 2 they read the X-ray systematically and name a malignant effusion from lung cancer as the leading diagnosis, with reasoned differentials. They set a COPD oxygen target, plan ultrasound-guided aspiration with the right fluid tests and a contrast CT, admit him, and answer "Is it cancer?" honestly without false certainty.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history and misses the weight loss or haemoptysis. They may not quantify the smoking or may examine the chest without percussing. They may call the X-ray "consolidation" or "heart failure" and order high-flow oxygen without a target. They may plan to drain the effusion completely at once, or forget cytology. Reassuring him that it is "probably nothing", or bluntly telling him he has cancer, is a communication concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: a malignant pleural effusion, probably from lung cancer

Sam has a large right pleural effusion. The most likely cause is malignancy, and the most likely primary is lung cancer. The key features are:

  • 5 months of progressive breathlessness that his COPD inhalers do not help
  • 20 kg of unintentional weight loss, anorexia, night sweats, chills and malaise
  • blood-tinged sputum
  • a hoarse voice, suggesting recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement by tumour or mediastinal nodes. Inhaled corticosteroid dysphonia (the fluticasone in his Trelegy) is a benign alternative, but new hoarseness persisting beyond 3 weeks in a smoker is a lung cancer red flag; vocal cord palsy can be confirmed at laryngoscopy
  • finger clubbing, which COPD alone does not cause
  • a hard supraclavicular node
  • a 50 pack-year smoking history in a 72-year-old man

A pleural effusion is fluid between the parietal and visceral pleura. The common causes are congestive heart failure, pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion) and malignancy.

The history

  • Breathlessness: onset, course, exercise tolerance then and now, and response to treatment.
  • Red flags for lung cancer: weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness, night sweats, fevers, malaise, anorexia and fatigue.
  • Differentials in other systems: heart failure (orthopnoea, PND, oedema), COPD exacerbation (change in cough, sputum or wheeze, drowsiness or confusion from hypercapnia) and pneumonia (fever, pleuritic pain, sick contacts).
  • Risk factors: smoking in pack-years, passive smoke, COPD, family history, radon and age. Occupational asbestos exposure (for example, brake linings) raises the risk of both lung cancer and mesothelioma. Ask about TB risk (country of birth, travel, contacts, past TB).
  • Before a pleural procedure: anticoagulants and antiplatelets.

The examination

A large effusion causes:

  • reduced expansion on the affected side
  • stony dull percussion
  • absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance, sometimes with bronchial breathing just above the fluid
  • a trachea pushed away from the effusion, as here

If a very large effusion causes no shift, think of collapse of the lung beneath it from an obstructing tumour, or a mediastinum fixed by tumour. Also look for cachexia, clubbing, lymph nodes, and the signs of heart failure and liver disease, which cause transudates.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 are in the yellow zone, with a rising RR and heart rate, so he needs a clinical review. For a patient with COPD, the TSANZ oxygen target is SpO2 88 to 92%. His 92% on room air needs no oxygen for now.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia only.
  • Bloods: anaemia, thrombocytosis, a raised CRP and low albumin fit chronic illness or malignancy. A normal troponin and NT-proBNP argue against ACS and heart failure. Normal clotting, an adequate platelet count and normal renal function make aspiration and contrast CT safe. The venous gas shows no hypercapnia. Serum protein and LDH are needed alongside the pleural fluid for Light's criteria.
  • Chest X-ray: a large right effusion up to the 2nd anterior rib with mediastinal shift to the left. The left lung is clear and the left costophrenic angle is sharp. The underlying lung cannot be seen, so a CT is needed.

Transudate or exudate

Transudates come from systemic factors (raised hydrostatic pressure or low oncotic pressure): heart failure, cirrhosis, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic syndrome, mitral stenosis, hypothyroidism and peritoneal dialysis.

Exudates come from local inflammation and increased capillary permeability: pneumonia, malignancy, TB, PE, rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune pleuritis, benign asbestos effusion, pancreatitis, post-MI and post-CABG.

Light's criteria classify the fluid as an exudate if any one of these is met:

  • pleural fluid to serum protein ratio above 0.5
  • pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio above 0.6
  • pleural fluid LDH above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH

Pleural fluid analysis

  • Appearance.
  • Protein and LDH, with paired serum levels.
  • Cell count and differential.
  • Cytology.
  • Gram stain and culture, plus acid-fast bacilli if TB is possible.
  • pH: below 7.2 in rheumatoid effusions, advanced malignancy and empyema.
  • Glucose: low in empyema, rheumatoid arthritis, TB and malignancy.
  • Amylase if pancreatitis is possible.

A negative cytology does not exclude malignancy. A pleural biopsy or tissue from elsewhere (a node, or the primary at bronchoscopy or EBUS) may be needed.

Management

  1. Supportive: sit him upright, monitor him, give oxygen to the COPD target and escalate to a senior.
  2. Aspiration: ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration by an experienced clinician is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Remove no more than about 1.5 L at a time to limit the risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
  3. Imaging: a contrast CT of the chest, ideally before the effusion is fully drained, to look for a primary tumour, nodes, pleural thickening or nodularity, and metastases.
  4. Diagnosis and disposition: admit and refer to the respiratory team and the lung cancer multidisciplinary team for a tissue diagnosis and staging.

Treatment by cause:

  • Heart failure: a loop diuretic and daily weights, with therapeutic thoracentesis if the effusion is large.
  • Parapneumonic effusion: antibiotics, with drainage of any empyema or complicated effusion (for example, pus or a low pH).
  • Malignant effusion: the prognosis is poor. Drain it if it causes symptoms. It often re-accumulates, so definitive options are talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter, chosen with the patient.

Offer smoking cessation (NRT in hospital, Quitline), dietitian review and social support, because he lives alone.

Breaking uncertain news

When he asks "Is it cancer?", answer honestly that cancer is a real possibility and explain what tests will show. Avoid both false reassurance and premature certainty, check his understanding, and offer to involve his family.

Safety netting and follow-up

He should tell the nurse at once about:

  • worsening breathlessness, chest pain, more blood in his sputum or feeling faint
  • after drainage: chest tightness, a persistent cough or new breathlessness (re-expansion oedema or pneumothorax)

Before discharge, the inpatient team reviews the fluid and CT results and the MDT sets a plan. His GP receives a letter. He needs to know the fluid can come back, so he should return to ED, or call 000, if the breathlessness returns.
points: In a smoker with progressive breathlessness, ask directly about weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness and night sweats, and quantify smoking in pack-years (20 a day for 50 years is 50 pack-years).

A large effusion gives reduced expansion, stony dullness, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance, with the trachea pushed away. Clubbing is not caused by COPD and should prompt a search for lung cancer.
In COPD, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88 to 92% (TSANZ); do not give high-concentration oxygen by reflex.

Ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic. Remove no more than about 1.5 L at once, and send protein and LDH (with serum levels for Light's criteria), pH, glucose, cell count, cytology, and Gram stain and culture with AFB.
Get a contrast CT of the chest, ideally before full drainage, and refer to the lung cancer MDT. Recurrent malignant effusions are managed with talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter.
Answer "Is it cancer?" honestly: it is a real possibility, not yet confirmed. Explain the next steps in plain words and safety-net for re-accumulation.
